p.src: Now, when Feng Su heard that the constables had summoned him, he hurried out, smiling deferentially, to ask what they wanted. The men merely shouted, “Bring Master Zhen out at once!” Feng Su hastily replied with a placating smile, “My humble surname is Feng, not Zhen. Only my former son-in-law was surnamed Zhen, but he became a monk a year or two ago. Could it be him you are asking after?” The constables said, “We know nothing about any ‘Zhen’ or ‘Jia,’ true or false. We have come to inquire at His Excellency’s command. Since the man is your son-in-law, you must come with us and report to His Excellency in person, so that we need not run about for nothing.” With that, they allowed Feng Su no further words but crowded around and hustled him away. Everyone in the Feng household was alarmed, not knowing what this might portend.

p.src: That night, at about the second watch, Feng Su finally returned, beside himself with joy. Everyone hurried to ask what had happened. He explained, “It turns out that the newly appointed prefect is surnamed Jia and named Hua. He comes from Huzhou and was once acquainted with my son-in-law. Just now, as he passed our gate, he saw the maid Jiaoxing buying thread and assumed that my son-in-law had moved here. I told him the whole story. His Excellency sighed sorrowfully for a while and then asked about his granddaughter. I said that she had disappeared while watching the lanterns. His Excellency said, ‘Never fear. I shall send runners to search until they are sure to find and bring her back.’ After we had talked for a while, he even gave me two taels of silver as I was leaving.” When Madam Zhen heard this, she could not help feeling grieved. Nothing more occurred that night. Early the next day, Yucun sent two packets of silver and four bolts of brocade to thank Madam Zhen. He also sent Feng Su a confidential letter, asking him to approach Madam Zhen on his behalf and request Jiaoxing as a second wife. Feng Su was so delighted that he scarcely knew what to do with himself. Eager for the chance to ingratiate himself, he pressed the matter upon his daughter with all his might until she consented; then, under cover of night, Jiaoxing was carried to Yucun’s residence in a small sedan chair. Yucun’s delight need hardly be described. He presented Feng Su with a hundred pieces of gold and gave Madam Zhen many gifts besides, instructing that she be well provided for while they awaited news of her daughter. Feng Su then returned home, and nothing further need be said of it.

That one chance glance had brought about this whole affair—an extraordinary turn of fate she herself could never have foreseen. Who would have thought that fortune would favor her twice over? Within a year of joining Yucun she gave birth to a son; another six months later, Yucun’s principal wife suddenly fell ill and died, whereupon he raised Jiaoxing from concubine to lawful wife. p.src: After Shiyin gave Yucun the silver that year, Yucun set out for the capital on the sixteenth. When the great examination was held, fortune favored him beyond expectation: he passed as a Presented Scholar, received an appointment outside the capital, and had now been promoted to prefect of this very district. Though highly capable, he was not free from greed and cruelty; moreover, he relied on his talents to show contempt for his superiors, so his fellow officials all looked askance at him. Before a year had passed, his superiors found an opening and drew up a memorial accusing him of being “crafty by nature, arbitrarily altering rites and regulations, trading on a reputation for probity while secretly associating with men as savage as tigers and wolves, thereby creating endless trouble in the district and making life unbearable for the people,” among other charges. The emperor was enraged and at once endorsed his dismissal. When the ministry’s order arrived, every official in the prefecture rejoiced. Though Yucun felt deeply humiliated and resentful, his face betrayed not the slightest bitterness. He remained as cheerful and smiling as ever, handed over his official duties, and sent the modest fortune accumulated during his years in office, together with his family and servants, back to his native place. Once everything had been properly settled, he himself cast care to the winds and went roaming among the celebrated sights of the realm.

p.src: One day his travels happened to bring him again to the region of Weiyang, where he heard that Lin Ruhai had been appointed this year’s Salt Commissioner. This Lin Ruhai’s surname was Lin, his personal name Hai, and his courtesy name Ruhai. He had placed third in the previous metropolitan examination and had since risen to the office of Censor of the Lantai. A native of Gusu, he had now been appointed by imperial decree as Salt Inspector and had held the post for just over a month. One of Lin Ruhai’s ancestors had inherited the rank of marquis, and by Ruhai’s generation the family line had continued for five generations. Originally the title was to be inherited for only three generations, but the present emperor’s abundant grace and virtue far surpassed those of earlier reigns, and by a special act of favor Ruhai’s father was allowed to inherit it for one further generation; but Ruhai himself entered official life through the examinations. Thus, though theirs was a house of hereditary rank, it was also a family steeped in learning. Unfortunately, the collateral branches of the Lin family had never flourished, and its descendants were few. Though there were several related households, they were only distant clansmen of Ruhai’s generation, and none belonged to a close direct line. Ruhai was now forty years old. His only son had reached the age of three, but had unfortunately died the previous year. Though he had several concubines, fate had denied him another son, and nothing could be done about it. His principal wife, née Jia, had borne him just one daughter, whose childhood name was Daiyu and who was now five years old. Having no son, husband and wife treasured her like a jewel. Seeing, moreover, that she was intelligent and graceful, they decided to teach her to read and recognize a few characters, treating her in some measure as a foster son so as to ease the sorrow of having no child at their knees.

p.src: At this time Yucun happened to catch a chill and lay ill at an inn; nearly a month passed before he gradually recovered. Since he was physically exhausted and his traveling funds were also running short, he was looking for a suitable place where he might settle temporarily and rest. Fortunately, two old friends of his were living in the area. When he heard that the Salt Commissioner wished to engage a private tutor, Yucun enlisted their help, secured the position, and thus found a means of supporting himself. Best of all, there was only one girl to teach, attended by two maidservants who studied with her. The pupil was young and exceedingly delicate, and there was no fixed amount of schoolwork required, so the post was remarkably undemanding. Almost another year passed. Then, unexpectedly, the girl’s mother, Lady Jia, succumbed to an illness. The girl attended her mother with medicine and broth and then mourned her with the fullest devotion; Yucun therefore considered leaving the post and seeking some other occupation. Lin Ruhai, however, wished his daughter to continue her studies during mourning and therefore kept him on. Recently, overcome by excessive grief, the girl—always frail and sickly—had suffered a recurrence of an old complaint and had consequently missed her lessons for several days. With nothing to occupy him, Yucun would go out for a leisurely walk after meals whenever the weather was clear and mild.

p.src: One day, he happened to wander beyond the city walls, intending to enjoy the rustic scenery. Strolling wherever his feet led him, he suddenly came to a place encircled by hills and winding water, thick with luxuriant woods and deep bamboo groves. Through them he could dimly see a temple whose gateway and alleys were crumbling and whose walls had fallen into decay. Above the entrance hung a plaque bearing the three characters “Temple of Penetrating Wisdom,” while beside the gate was an old, tattered couplet: “Though wealth remains when life is done, one forgets to stay one’s hand; only when no road lies ahead does one think of turning back.” On reading it, Yucun thought, “The wording of these two lines may be plain, but their meaning is profound. I have visited many famous mountains and great monasteries, yet I have never encountered such a saying. There may well be someone inside who has suffered a great reversal in life. Why not go in and see?” With this thought he went inside, but found only a decrepit old monk cooking porridge. At the sight of him, Yucun paid him little heed. When he tried asking him a few questions, however, the old monk proved both deaf and muddle-headed; his teeth were gone, his tongue was slow, and his replies bore no relation to what was asked.

p.src: Growing impatient, Yucun came out again and decided to buy a few cups of wine at the village tavern to heighten his enjoyment of the countryside, so he strolled leisurely toward it. Just as he was about to enter, one of the customers drinking inside rose with a hearty laugh and came out to meet him, exclaiming, “What a remarkable encounter! What a remarkable encounter!” Yucun looked closely and recognized Leng Zixing, an acquaintance from his days in the capital who dealt in antiques there. Yucun greatly admired Leng Zixing as an able and enterprising man, while Zixing valued the prestige of Yucun’s learning; thus they found each other congenial in conversation and were especially well suited as friends. Yucun hastened to ask with a smile, “When did you arrive here, my dear friend? I had no idea at all. To meet you by chance today is truly a fortunate turn of fate.” Zixing replied, “I returned home at the end of last year. As I must soon go back to the capital, I stopped along the way to speak with an old friend here, and he was kind enough to ask me to remain for a few more days. I have no urgent business, so I shall linger for a couple of days and set out around the middle of the month. My friend had business to attend to today, so I wandered here to rest my feet. Who could have expected such a happy coincidence!” As he spoke, he invited Yucun to sit at his table and had fresh wine and dishes brought out. The two drank at their ease and chatted about all that had happened since they parted.

p.src: Yucun asked, “Has there been any news in the capital lately?” Zixing replied, “Nothing of much consequence, except that a minor curiosity has occurred in the household of your distinguished kinsmen.” Yucun laughed. “None of my clan lives in the capital. How can you say that?” Zixing laughed. “Since you share the same surname, are you not members of the same clan?” Yucun asked which family he meant. Zixing replied, “Surely the Jia family of the Rongguo Mansion does no disgrace to your illustrious lineage?” Yucun laughed. “Ah, so you mean that family. Come to think of it, our humble clan is very numerous. Ever since Jia Fu of the Eastern Han, its branches have flourished and spread through every province; who could investigate them all one by one? As for the Rongguo branch, however, we are indeed recorded in the same genealogy. But theirs is such an illustrious house that we could hardly presume upon the connection; consequently, we have grown ever more distant and scarcely recognize one another now.” Zixing sighed. “You should not speak so, sir. Both the Ningguo and Rongguo houses are declining now, and things are no longer as they once were.” Yucun said, “In former days both the Ningguo and Rongguo households were exceedingly populous. How could they have declined so quickly?” Leng Zixing replied, “Indeed they were. It is a long story.” Yucun said, “Last year I went to the Jinling region to view the remains of the Six Dynasties. One day I entered the Stone City and passed the gates of their old residences. The Ningguo Mansion stood east of the street and the Rongguo Mansion west; the two residences adjoined each other and occupied more than half the street. Though the great gates were deserted and no one was about, a glance over the surrounding walls showed halls, pavilions, and towers still rising in imposing grandeur. Even the trees and rocks in the gardens behind remained lush and richly verdant. How could that look like a family in decline?” Leng Zixing laughed. “And you a graduate of the highest imperial examination! You understand nothing after all. The ancients said, ‘A centipede does not stiffen even when dead.’ Although they are no longer as prosperous as in former years, their bearing is still quite unlike that of an ordinary official family. The household grows more populous by the day and its affairs more numerous, yet among masters and servants, high and low, there are plenty who enjoy wealth, rank, and ease, but not one who knows how to plan and manage. Nor can they bring themselves to reduce their daily pomp and expenditure. Thus, although the outer framework has not yet greatly collapsed, their resources within are nearly exhausted. Yet that is only a minor matter. There is a graver one: who would have thought that in a family accustomed to the ringing of bells and feasting from tripods, a clan devoted to letters, poetry, and the classics, the sons and grandsons should now prove worse with every generation!” Yucun was astonished to hear this. “How could a family steeped in poetry and ritual fail to educate its children properly? I cannot speak for other houses, but the Ningguo and Rongguo mansions in particular have always been renowned for knowing how to raise their sons.”

p.src: Zixing sighed. “Those are precisely the two houses I was speaking of. Let me tell you: in former days, the Duke of Ningguo and the Duke of Rongguo were brothers born of the same mother. The Duke of Ningguo was the elder and had four sons. After his death, Jia Daihua inherited his title and had two sons of his own. The elder, Jia Fu, died at eight or nine, leaving only the younger, Jia Jing, to inherit the title. Nowadays Jia Jing is wholly devoted to Daoism: he cares only for compounding elixirs and refining cinnabar, and pays no heed to anything else. Fortunately, he had fathered a son in his younger days, named Jia Zhen. Since his father was bent on becoming an immortal, he yielded the title to him. His father refuses to return to the ancestral home and merely consorts with Daoist priests outside the capital. Master Zhen, for his part, has a son named Jia Rong, who is only sixteen this year. Old Master Jing now pays no attention to anything at all. As for Master Zhen, he has no intention of studying and thinks of nothing but endless pleasure. He has turned the Ningguo mansion upside down, yet no one dares restrain him. Now listen while I tell you of the Rongguo house, for that is where the strange affair I mentioned occurred. After the Duke of Rongguo died, his eldest son, Jia Daishan, inherited the title. He married a daughter of the hereditary Marquis Shi’s family of Jinling and had two sons: the elder, Jia She, and the younger, Jia Zheng. Daishan has long since passed away, though the Dowager Lady is still living. The eldest son, Jia She, holds the hereditary title. The younger, Jia Zheng, was passionately fond of books from childhood and was his grandfather’s favorite. His family originally intended him to enter official life through the civil examinations, but as Daishan lay dying, he submitted a memorial. Out of regard for his former minister, the Emperor not only allowed the eldest son to inherit the title but asked how many other sons there were and ordered them presented at court immediately. He then exceptionally conferred on Jia Zheng the rank of Department Secretary and directed him to train in a ministry. He has now risen to Vice Director. Jia Zheng’s wife, Lady Wang, first bore a son named Jia Zhu. He qualified as a licentiate at fourteen, married and fathered a child before he was twenty, but then fell ill and died. Her second child was a daughter, born on New Year’s Day—strange enough in itself. Later she unexpectedly bore another son, and stranger still, the moment he emerged from the womb he had in his mouth a lustrous, many-colored piece of jade covered with writing. He was therefore named Baoyu. Would you not call that a strange and novel affair?”

Her second child was a daughter, born on New Year’s Day—strange enough in itself. Later she unexpectedly bore another son, and stranger still, the moment he emerged from the womb he had in his mouth a lustrous, many-colored piece of jade covered with writing. He was therefore named Baoyu.
Would you not call that a strange and novel affair?”

p.src: Yucun smiled. “It is strange indeed. I fear this boy can be no ordinary being.” Zixing sneered. “Everyone says so, and that is why his grandmother has treasured him like a precious jewel from the first. When he turned one, Master Zheng wished to test his future inclinations, so he set before him a great array of every sort of object in the world and let him choose among them. To everyone’s surprise, he took none of them, but reached only for rouge, powder, hairpins, and bracelets. Master Zheng flew into a rage and said, ‘He will grow up to be nothing but a debauchee!’ From then on, he took a great dislike to the boy. Only old Lady Shi continued to regard him as dearer than life itself. Yet here is another strange thing: now that he is seven or eight, though extraordinarily mischievous, he is so clever and quick-witted that not one boy in a hundred can compare with him. Even the childish things he says are peculiar. He says, ‘Girls are made of water, while men are made of mud. When I see girls, I feel refreshed and pure; when I see men, I feel assailed by foulness and stench.’ Is that not laughable? There is no doubt he will grow into a lecher!” Yucun looked astonished and grave and hurriedly stopped him. “No! It is a pity that none of you understands the origin of such a person. I expect even our respected elder Master Zheng has mistakenly taken him for a lustful fiend and lecher. Unless one has read widely and understood worldly affairs, investigated things to extend one’s knowledge, and cultivated the power to fathom the Way and penetrate its mysteries, one cannot comprehend it.”

p.src: Seeing him speak with such gravity, Zixing hastened to ask him to explain. Yucun said, “When Heaven and Earth bring forth human beings, apart from those of supreme benevolence and those of supreme wickedness, all the rest differ little from one another. Those of supreme benevolence are born in response to an auspicious age; those of supreme wickedness, in response to a time of calamity. The auspicious influence arises when the world is well governed; calamity arises when the world is imperiled. Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Kings Wen and Wu, the Dukes of Zhou and Shao, Confucius, Mencius, Dong Zhongshu, Han Yu, Zhou Dunyi, the Cheng brothers, Zhang Zai, and Zhu Xi were all born in response to an auspicious age. Chiyou, Gonggong, Jie, Zhou, the First Emperor, Wang Mang, Cao Cao, Huan Wen, An Lushan, Qin Hui, and their like were all born in response to calamity. The supremely benevolent bring order to the realm; the supremely wicked throw it into turmoil. Clarity, purity, vitality, and refinement are the upright vital force of Heaven and Earth, inherited by the benevolent; cruelty, perversity, and waywardness are their corrupt vital force, inherited by the wicked. In our present dynasty, whose fortune flourishes and whose mandate endures, in this peaceful age of effortless government, those endowed with the clear and refined vital force abound everywhere, from the imperial court down to the common fields. The remaining refined essence, having nowhere particular to settle, becomes sweet dew and gentle winds, spreading harmoniously to nourish all within the four seas. But the corrupt force of cruelty and perversity cannot spread beneath the bright heavens and transforming sun. It therefore congeals and accumulates in deep ditches and vast ravines. Now and then, stirred by wind or driven by clouds, it begins faintly to move and respond. If the merest thread of it escapes by chance and happens to encounter a passing current of refined spiritual force, the upright will not admit the corrupt, while the corrupt envies the upright. Neither will yield. It is like wind, water, thunder, and lightning meeting within the earth: unable either to dissolve or give way, they must clash and erupt before they can exhaust themselves. Thus this mingled force must enter a human being and expend itself completely before it can disperse. If a man or woman happens to be born endowed with this force, such a person can neither rise to become benevolent and noble nor sink to become utterly vicious and wicked. Set among countless millions, such a person’s intelligence, talent, vitality, and refinement rise above them all, yet in waywardness, perversity, and disregard for ordinary human conventions, that person falls below them all. Born into a wealthy ducal or marquisal family, such people become infatuated devotees of love; born into a poor but cultivated family of books and poetry, they become lofty recluses and men of distinction. Even if by chance born into a humble family of scant fortune, they can never become common runners or sturdy servants, meekly submitting to the control and command of mediocrities; instead, they are bound to become extraordinary performers or celebrated courtesans. Such were, in former ages, Xu You, Tao Qian, Ruan Ji, Ji Kang, Liu Ling, the Wang and Xie clans, Gu Hutou, the Last Emperor of Chen, Emperor Ming of Tang, Emperor Huizong of Song, Liu Tingzhi, Wen Feiqing, Mi Nangong, Shi Manqing, Liu Qiqing, and Qin Shaoyou; and in more recent times, Ni Yunlin, Tang Bohu, and Zhu Zhishan. So too were Li Guinian, Huang Fanchuo, Jing Xinmo, Zhuo Wenjun, Hongfu, Xue Tao, Cui Yingying, and Chaoyun. All were people of essentially the same nature, differing only in their circumstances.”

Do you know the Zhen family in Jinling—the family of the imperial commissioner who serves as President of the Ministry of Benevolent Governance for Jinling Province?” Zixing said, “Who does not know them! I myself have been acquainted with that family for quite some time.”

u.src: There is no need to look far afield. Do you know the Zhen family in Jinling—the family of the imperial commissioner who serves as President of the Ministry of Benevolent Governance for Jinling Province?”
Zixing said, “Who does not know them!

The two households are on the most intimate terms.
I myself have been acquainted with that family for quite some time.”

p.src: Yucun smiled. “Last year, when I was in Jinling, someone recommended me for a tutoring post in the Zhen household. When I entered and observed the household, I found that despite their lofty rank, they were wealthy yet respectful of propriety; it was indeed a rare and desirable post. But although my pupil was only beginning his education, he caused me more trouble than a student preparing for the civil-service examinations. What he said was more amusing still: ‘I must have two girls study beside me before I can recognize the characters and understand them clearly. Otherwise, my mind becomes muddled.’ He would also often tell the pageboys attending him, ‘The two words “young lady” are supremely noble and supremely pure—more exalted and incomparable even than the sacred names Amitabha Buddha and the Celestial Worthy of the Primordial Beginning! Your filthy mouths and foul tongues must never profane those words. Be sure to remember that. Whenever you wish to utter them, you must first rinse your mouths with pure water and fragrant tea. If you slip up, your teeth will be bored through and your cheeks pierced.’ His cruelty, impatience, obstinacy, mischief, foolishness, and infatuation were all extraordinary. Yet as soon as lessons ended and he went in to see the girls, he became so gentle and peaceable, intelligent and refined, that he seemed another person entirely. For this reason, his honored father has several times beaten him almost to death, but nothing could make him change. Whenever the beating became too painful to bear, he would cry out wildly, ‘Elder sister! Younger sister!’ Later, I heard that the girls inside teased him: ‘Why do you keep calling for your sisters whenever the beating grows severe? Can it be that you want your sisters to intercede and beg forgiveness for you? Are you not ashamed of yourself?’ His answer was delightful. He said, ‘When the pain is acute, it seems possible that merely crying “elder sister” and “younger sister” might ease it. Once, after I called out, the pain truly seemed to disappear. Thus I discovered a secret remedy: whenever the pain becomes unbearable, I call out for my sisters again and again.’ Is that not ridiculous? Moreover, his grandmother doted upon him blindly and would humiliate the tutor and scold her son whenever anything concerned her grandson. So I resigned my post and left. I am now tutoring in the household of Lord Lin, the Salt Censor. You see, a boy like that can never preserve the foundations laid by his forefathers or heed the admonitions of his teachers and elders. It is only a pity, for his several sisters are all exceptionally fine.”

p.src: Zixing said, “The three girls now in the Jia household are quite remarkable too. Master Zheng’s eldest daughter is named Yuanchun. On account of her virtue, filial devotion, talent, and character, she has been selected to enter the palace as a female secretary. The second young lady, Yingchun, was born to Master She’s first wife; the third, Tanchun, is Master Zheng’s daughter by a concubine; and the fourth, Xichun, is the full sister of Master Zhen of the Ningguo house. Because the Lady Dowager Shi is exceedingly fond of her granddaughters, they all stay with their grandmother and study together. I hear that every one of them is admirable.” Yucun said, “What is even finer about the Zhen family’s custom is that their daughters’ personal names follow the naming pattern of the men’s, rather than using separately chosen, florid characters such as ‘spring,’ ‘red,’ ‘fragrance,’ or ‘jade,’ as other families do. Why, then, does the Jia family delight in this commonplace convention?” Zixing replied, “That is not so. The eldest young lady was born on the first day of the first lunar month and was therefore named Yuanchun; only after that were the others named with the character ‘chun.’ The women of the preceding generation were indeed named according to the same pattern as their brothers. There is living proof: the wife of your present employer, Lord Lin, is the full sister of Lords She and Zheng of the Rongguo house, and before her marriage she was called Jia Min. If you do not believe me, go back and make careful inquiries.” Yucun struck the table and laughed. “No wonder whenever my young pupil comes across the character ‘min’ in a book, she invariably pronounces it ‘mi,’ and whenever she must write it, she omits one or two strokes. I had begun to wonder about it. Now that I have heard what you say, there can be no doubt that this was the reason. No wonder this pupil of mine is so distinctive in speech and bearing, quite unlike the girls of today. I supposed that only an extraordinary mother could have borne such a daughter. Now that I know she is a granddaughter of the Rongguo house, there is nothing surprising about it. Sadly, her mother passed away only last month.” Zixing sighed. “Of the four sisters of that older generation, she was the youngest, and now she too is gone. Not one of the sisters of the older generation remains. We can only wait and see what sort of husbands the younger generation will marry.”

p.src: Yucun said, “Indeed. We said just now that Lord Zheng has a son born with jade in his mouth, as well as a frail grandson left by his eldest son. Can it be that Master She has no son at all?” Zixing said, “After Lord Zheng had his jade-bearing son, one of his concubines bore him another, though I do not know what sort of boy he is. At present he has two sons and one grandson, though no one knows what will become of them. As for Lord She, he too has two sons. The elder is named Jia Lian and is now about twenty. In a marriage between relations, he took as his wife a niece of Lady Wang, Lord Zheng’s wife, and they have now been married for two years. Master Lian has purchased the nominal rank of sub-prefect. He too refuses to study, but he is adaptable in worldly affairs and speaks with tact. He therefore lives at present in the household of his uncle, Lord Zheng, helping to manage domestic business. Yet since he married his worthy wife, everyone in the household, high and low, has praised her, while Master Lian himself has been put entirely in the shade. They say she is exceptionally beautiful, forthright and fluent in speech, and extraordinarily subtle and discerning of mind—a woman whom not one man in ten thousand could equal.”
